title: What first aid training do Australian workplaces need?
description: First aid training in Australian workplaces: model WHS Regulation 42, the model Code ratios, annual CPR and three yearly refreshers, and Victoria's own code.
shortAnswer: In Australian jurisdictions that have adopted the model WHS laws, Regulation 42 of the WHS Regulations requires a business to ensure an adequate number of workers are trained to administer first aid, or have access to trained people. The model Code of Practice recommends a nationally recognized Provide First Aid qualification, CPR refresher training every year, requalification every three years, and one first aider per 50, 25 or 10 workers depending on risk. Victoria uses its own compliance code.
keyTakeaways: Model WHS Regulation 42 requires a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) to provide first aid equipment, access to first aid facilities, and an adequate number of trained first aiders, having regard to the nature of the work, hazards, size and location of the workplace, and the number and composition of people there.

The model Code of Practice: First aid in the workplace (July 2019) recommends that first aiders hold a nationally recognised Statement of Attainment for the Provide First Aid unit of competency from a registered training organization (RTO), or equivalent.

The Code recommends CPR refresher training annually and renewal of first aid qualifications every three years. These are recommendations ("should"), but codes are admissible in court as evidence of what is reasonably practicable.
Recommended ratios are one first aider per 50 workers in low risk workplaces, one per 25 in high risk workplaces, and one per 10 in remote high risk workplaces.

Victoria has not adopted the model WHS laws. Employers there work under section 21 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic) and WorkSafe Victoria's 2021 compliance code, which uses different first aid officer ratios but the same refresher intervals.
jurisdiction: Australia: Commonwealth and the states and territories that have adopted the model WHS laws; Victoria under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic)
regulator: State, territory and Commonwealth WHS regulators (Safe Work Australia maintains the model laws but does not regulate); WorkSafe Victoria in Victoria
appliesTo: Every person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU) in a jurisdiction that has adopted the model WHS laws
Employers in Victoria, under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic)
Officers, such as directors, who must exercise due diligence over first aid arrangements
Workers trained as first aiders, and all workers who must know how to access first aid

sections.heading: Which law requires first aid training in Australian workplaces?

blocks.text: As at November 2026, in every jurisdiction except Victoria, the duty sits in each jurisdiction's WHS Regulations, based on Regulation 42 of the model Work Health and Safety Regulations. [Safe Work Australia](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/law-and-regulation/model-whs-laws) states that the model laws have been implemented in all jurisdictions except Victoria, that some jurisdictions have made variations, and that each must implement the laws separately for them to be legally binding.

As quoted in the [model Code of Practice](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-10/code_of_practice_-_first_aid_in_the_workplace_July%202019.pdf), Regulation 42 requires a PCBU to ensure the provision of first aid equipment, that each worker has access to it, access to facilities for administering first aid, and "an adequate number of workers are trained to administer first aid, or workers have access to an adequate number of other people who have been trained to administer first aid." Regulation 42(3) lists the matters the PCBU must have regard to: the nature of the work, the nature of the hazards, the size and location of the workplace, and the number and composition of workers and other people.

The detail on training comes from the model Code of Practice: First aid in the workplace, first published in July 2012 and current in its July 2019 version. Codes are approved under section 274 of the WHS Act, but a model code has legal effect only once a jurisdiction approves it, so [Safe Work Australia advises](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-first-aid-workplace) checking with the local regulator. Approved codes are admissible in court, and courts may rely on them to decide what is reasonably practicable.

blocks.title: Must versus should
blocks.text: The Code uses "must" for legal requirements and "should" for recommended courses of action. The CPR and requalification intervals and the first aider ratios are "should" recommendations. A business can follow another method that gives an equivalent or higher standard of health and safety, but it then needs to be able to show that.

sections.heading: What qualification should workplace first aiders hold?

blocks.text: The Code says that, as a minimum, first aiders should hold a nationally recognised Statement of Attainment issued by a registered training organization (RTO) for the nationally endorsed unit of competency Provide First Aid, or a course providing equivalent skills. A higher level of training may be needed for the risks identified.

items: work that is remote or isolated
risks from dangerous substances such as cyanide or arsenic
specialist first aid equipment or a first aid room at the workplace
children present in the workplace
identified psychological risks
workers with existing medical conditions that may require first aid, in which case first aiders should be trained to respond to those conditions

blocks.text: First aiders can be the business's own workers or people from another business, for example a business sharing the same building, provided the PCBU consults, cooperates and coordinates with that business so first aiders are available whenever its workers are working, including shifts and overtime.

sections.heading: How often must first aid training be refreshed?

blocks.text: The Code recommends CPR refresher training every year and renewal of first aid qualifications every three years. In its words: "Refresher training in CPR should be carried out annually and first aid qualifications should be renewed every three years." The purpose, according to the Code, is to refresh knowledge and skills and to confirm competence.

WorkSafe Victoria's compliance code uses the same intervals for first aid officers. A training system therefore needs two clocks per first aider: a 12 month CPR cycle and a 36 month qualification cycle, both counted from the date on the Statement of Attainment rather than the course booking.

sections.heading: How many trained first aiders does a workplace need?

blocks.text: The model Code recommends ratios by risk level, then refines them through a five step assessment. The ratios are a starting point, not a cap.

sections.heading: What must all workers be told about first aid?

blocks.text: Every worker must receive the information needed to protect their health and safety, and the Code says this should include where first aid equipment and facilities are, who the first aiders are and where to find them, and the procedure to follow when first aid is needed. It should be part of induction training and repeated when first aiders or facilities change, in a form that suits workers' language and literacy.

The Code also recommends written first aid procedures, which should include arrangements for first aiders' training and for workers' information, instruction and training. Emergency procedures should state each first aider's role by qualification, and both first aiders and supervisors should be instructed that first aiders must not exceed their training. Regulation 43 separately requires an emergency plan covering medical treatment and assistance. The Code recommends a mock first aid emergency as part of regular review.

Victoria regulates first aid under the general duty to provide adequate facilities for employees' welfare in section 21 of the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic), not under model Regulation 42. WorkSafe Victoria's [Compliance code: First aid in the workplace](https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/resources/compliance-code-first-aid-workplace) (Edition 1, November 2021) gives guidance, and an employer that follows it is treated as having complied with the duties it covers.

items: **Terminology.** The Victorian code uses "first aid officer" and "employer" rather than "first aider" and "PCBU".
**Two options.** Employers can follow a prescribed approach based on risk level and size, or a risk assessment approach, which large or complex workplaces need to use.

**Qualification.** First aid officers need, as a minimum, a nationally recognised Statement of Attainment from an RTO for Provide First Aid or equivalent, and higher risk workplaces may need Provide Advanced First Aid.
**Refreshers.** CPR training should be carried out annually and first aid qualifications renewed every three years, matching the model Code.
**Coverage.** Where possible at least one first aid officer should be available at any one time during operating hours, allowing for rosters, leave and flexible work.

blocks.text: National employers should keep a single first aid training standard but separate ratio calculations for Victorian sites. The related page on the [WHS duty to provide training](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training) explains the wider differences between the model WHS Act and Victoria's OHS Act.

sections.heading: How do you evidence first aid training compliance?

blocks.text: Keep records that show the first aid assessment, who the first aiders are, and that their training is current. The checklist below is original and illustrative.

items: A dated first aid assessment covering the four matters in Regulation 42(3), or the Victorian code's prescribed or risk assessment approach, reviewed when work changes.
A first aider register by site and shift, showing coverage for leave and overtime.
Each first aider's Statement of Attainment, unit of competency and issue date, with CPR and requalification due dates.
Records of any additional training for identified risks, such as remote work or specific medical conditions.
Induction records showing all workers were told where kits, facilities and first aiders are.
Written first aid procedures and the emergency plan, with mock emergency results.

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) with expiry tracking handles the two refresher clocks. Because a certificate shows only that a course was completed, organizations with higher risks often add [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) through drills. For setting and defending intervals, see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Regulation 42, the model Code recommendations and the Victorian compliance code as separate, jurisdiction tagged obligations linked to roles and sites. Each first aider role carries its competency, refresher intervals and assessment points, so a site's first aid coverage and any expiring qualifications can be reported from the same framework.

faqs.q: Is annual CPR refresher training a legal requirement in Australia?
faqs.a: Not directly. Regulation 42 requires an adequate number of trained first aiders. The model Code of Practice recommends annual CPR refreshers and three yearly requalification using the word "should". Where the Code is approved in a jurisdiction, courts can use it as evidence of what is reasonably practicable, so departing from it needs a documented equivalent standard.

faqs.q: Does every small business need a trained first aider?
faqs.a: Not always on site. The model Code recognizes that workers who work alone or in transit may not have a first aider present, but they must be able to access first aid, for example through a way to contact emergency services and training on how to respond. In Victoria, low risk micro-businesses with fewer than 10 employees follow separate recommendations.

faqs.q: Can we rely on another business's first aiders?
faqs.a: Yes, if arrangements are coordinated. The model Code allows a PCBU to give its workers access to first aiders from another business sharing the workplace, after consulting, cooperating and coordinating with that business. The first aiders must be available at the times the workers carry out work, including shifts and overtime.

faqs.q: Do the model WHS laws apply in Victoria?
faqs.a: No. Safe Work Australia states the model laws have been implemented in all jurisdictions except Victoria. Victorian employers follow the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 (Vic) and the Occupational Health and Safety Regulations 2017, with WorkSafe Victoria's 2021 first aid compliance code as guidance.
